content.body:
The first WTA 1000 of the 2026 Asian Swing on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz ended with a record-setting title run as Zheng Qinwen became the first home player to claim the China Open crown since the tournament's inception in 1994.

Zheng battled through four consecutive three-setters in her first four rounds, but did not concede a set in her last three matches -- which included a pair of Top 10 wins, over Elina Svitolina and Mirra Andreeva, to take her 2026 total to three. In total, she dropped 78 games en route to the trophy -- the most lost in any WTA 1000 or Tier I title run since the format's inception in 1990.

Only one Chinese player had previously made the Beijing final -- Chen Li-Ling, who was the runner-up to Wang Shi-Ting in 1994. Zheng's title run was the 13th time a Chinese player had won a WTA tournament on home soil, the first since her own 2023 Zhengzhou trophy, and the first at WTA 1000 level.

The former No. 4's sixth title overall continued her remarkable resurgence over the past two months. After undergoing elbow surgery last July and attempting to return at Beijing last year, Zheng's comeback proper started this February in the Middle East Swing. She compiled an 11-13 record through Toronto, where she lost her first qualifying match to Lanlana Tararudee. Following that tournament, the 24-year-old opted for an intense training block in Florida ahead of the US Open -- and since then, she has gone 14-2, including 8-1 in three-setters.

Just four months after her ranking fell to No. 160 in June, Zheng is already back in the Top 30. In the latest edition of the PIF WTA Rankings, she soars 31 places from No. 54 to No. 23.

Andreeva becomes youngest to make Top 3 debut in 21 years

Beijing runner-up Andreeva continued a career-best season which has already seen her become a Grand Slam champion for the first time by reaching her fifth final of the year -- a joint tour-leading number alongside Elena Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka and Jessica Pegula.

At 19 years and 166 days old, Andreeva is rewarded with her Top 3 debut this week, climbing two places from No. 5 to No. 3. She's the youngest player to enter the Top 3 since a 17-year-old Maria Sharapova in February 2005. Since then, only two other players have cracked the Top 3 as teenagers -- Caroline Wozniacki (19 years and 205 days old in February 2010) and Coco Gauff (19 years and 182 days old in September 2023).

Bartunkova enters Top 30, Charaeva makes Top 100 debut

Two early upsets shook the Beijing draw, and the two players who dealt them out are both rewarded by hitting new milestones this week.

Back in June, Nikola Bartunkova led Aryna Sabalenka 6-2, 4-0 in the Berlin quarterfinals, but was unable to close out the win. The 20-year-old Czech finished the job in the Beijing third round -- then went all the way to her first WTA 1000 semifinal, claiming another Top 10 win along the way over compatriot Karolina Muchova. Bartunkova, who ended 2025 ranked No. 130, climbs five places from No. 34 to make her Top 30 debut at No. 29 this week.

Alina Charaeva, the 2020 Roland Garros junior finalist, had already notched some career-best results in 2026 -- her first two WTA quarterfinals in Hamburg and Sao Paulo, her first WTA 125 title in Midland. But she had yet to defeat -- or even face -- a Top 30 opponent until her astonishing upset of new World No. 1 Elena Rybakina from a set and a break down in the Beijing second round. Charaeva went on to make the last 16, and this week jumps 20 places from No. 118 to make her Top 100 debut at No. 98. The 24-year-old becomes the second Armenian to be ranked in the Top 100 following Elina Avanesyan.

Mertens boosted by Beijing run; Jovic, Kraus, Sun up to new career highs

For nearly a decade, Elise Mertens has been a Top 50 mainstay: she first broke into it in July 2017, and has not fallen out since. The 30-year-old Belgian is taking another run at the career high of No. 12 she set in November 2018. At Wimbledon in July, she reached her first Grand Slam quarterfinal since the 2020 US Open. In Beijing last week, she made her first WTA 1000 semifinal since Madrid 2021.

Mertens' pair of Top 10 upsets in Beijing over Coco Gauff and Iga Swiatek also take her total this year to four -- the most Top 10 wins she's ever scored in a single season. She climbs five places from No. 19 to No. 14 this week, her highest position since May 2021.

Beijing quarterfinalists Elina Svitolina and Karolina Muchova both move up one place, to No. 6 and No. 7 respectively. For Svitolina, it's her highest ranking since September 2021.

Elsewhere, Iva Jovic and Sinja Kraus have both set new career highs after making the Beijing fourth round. Jovic, 18, is up to spots to No. 11 and Kraus, 24, jumps 20 to No. 75 after reaching the last 16 of a WTA 1000 event for the first time.

Junior No. 1 Sun Xinran made an impact on her WTA main-draw debut as a wild card. The Chinese 16-year-old, fresh off the US Open girls' title, upset Eva Lys and Cristina Bucsa -- the latter her first Top 50 win -- to make the Beijing third round. Sun became the first 2010-born player to win matches at WTA 1000 level, and this week she soars 164 places to enter the Top 500 for the first time at No. 418. She's now the second-highest ranked 2010-born player following Memphis champion Kristina Liutova at No. 116.

Jeanjean, Shubladze, Sramkova, Aksu rise following WTA 125 titles

Four WTA 125 events took place over the past two weeks, all on hard courts -- two in China (Jingshan followed by Suzhou) and two in Türkiye (Adana followed by Samsun).

In Jingshan, Alexandra Shubladze added her first WTA 125 title to her haul of five World Tennis trophies this season. The 21-year-old's run culminated in fine style as she notched her first career Top 100 win over Jessica Bouzas Maneiro 6-3, 6-2 in the final, extending her 2026 record to 55-15. Shubladze leaps 31 places to a new career high of No. 132.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Alexandra Shubladze (@alexandrashubladze5)

In Adana, Leolia Jeanjean battled to her first WTA 125 trophy, having lost her previous two finals at this level (Montevideo 2022, Colina 2025). The 31-year-old went to three sets in all five of her matches -- the only champion at WTA 125 level or above to do so this year so far -- saving two match points to defeat Melisa Ercan 3-6, 7-5, 6-4 in the second round and winning an all-French final 7-6(3), 4-6, 6-4 over Lois Boisson. Jeanjean rises 15 places to No. 94, just three spots beneath the career high of No. 91 that she set last August. Boisson, who entered the main draw as a lucky loser, climbs 16 places to No. 258.

Meanwhile, Erika Andreeva made the Adana semifinals as a qualifier, and climbs 32 places to No. 181 -- returning to the Top 200 for the first time since last August.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA125 Adana Open (@adana.open)

In Suzhou, Rebecca Sramkova lifted the trophy -- the former No. 33's first at any level since Hua Hin II 2024 -- with a 6-3, 6-1 defeat of qualifier Kyoka Okamura in the final, and climbs 18 places to No. 134. Okamura, who lost a high-quality first-round tilt in Singapore to eventual champion Leylah Fernandez three weeks ago, has maintained her form since -- the Japanese 31-year-old made the Jingshan quarterfinals ahead of her first WTA 125 final, and vaults 59 places from No. 303 to No. 244 this week.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Rebecca Sramkova (@rebbsramkova)

In Samsun, a home champion was crowned as Ayla Aksu defeated Lucrezia Stefanini 7-5, 2-6, 6-2 in the final to lift her first WTA 125 trophy. The 30-year-old is enjoying a career-best season in which she's also been the Figueira da Foz WTA 125 runner-up, won her first tour-level match since 2017 in Prague and made her Grand Slam qualifying debut at the US Open. This week, Aksu soars 54 places to a new career high of No. 156, while Stefanini is up 19 spots to No. 106.

Meanwhile, Anna Blinkova made the Samsun semifinals via a 6-3, 6-4 defeat of Bianca Andreescu in the quarterfinals, and is up 16 places to No. 73.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Ayla Aksu Kahraman (@aylaaksu6)

Other notable rankings movements

Tatjana Maria, +13 to No. 71 and Madison Brengle, +20 to No. 188: Maria, 39, and Brengle, 36, first played each other in Wimbledon qualifying in 2009. They met for a seventh time in the Templeton W100 final two weeks ago, with Maria winning for a sixth time in their rivalry 6-3, 6-4. Brengle, who followed her Templeton run by making the Lexington W50 semifinals last week, returns to the Top 200 for the first time since March 2024.

Ane Mintegi Del Olmo, +32 to No. 206: The 2021 Wimbledon junior champion has hit her stride in the pros this year. Mintegi Del Olmo is on a 10-match winning streak after collecting back-to-back Bulgarian W50 titles in Plovdiv and Burgas, and the 22-year-old Spaniard is up to a new career high.

Gao Xinyu, +24 to No. 220: The Chinese 28-year-old won her first tour-level match since the 2025 United Cup in Beijing last week -- and the first of her career on home soil -- upsetting Panna Udvardy in the Beijing first round.

Britt Du Pree, +40 to No. 281: The 19-year-old Dutchwoman makes her Top 300 debut after winning the Reims W35 title two weeks ago.

Alisa Oktiabreva, +125 to No. 311: Roland Garros junior champion Oktiabreva is on a 15-match winning streak after picking up three straight World Tennis titles -- two W35s in Santa Margherita di Pula, then last week's Heraklion W50. The 18-year-old Czech reached a career high of No. 280 this April.

Alena Kovackova, +67 to No. 340: Another 18-year-old Czech, Kovackova is up to a new career high after reaching the Santa Margherita di Pula W35 final (losing to Oktiabreva) and Burgas W50 semifinals.

Charo Esquiva Banuls, +95 to No. 449: Former junior No. 9 Esquiva Banuls is on a 10-match winning streak. The 18-year-old Spaniard won the first two professional titles of her career at the Yecla W50 and Baza W35 on home soil, and makes her Top 500 debut.

Astra Sharma, +605 to No. 576: After being sidelined for six months, former No. 84 Sharma returned to action in July, losing her first four matches back. But the 31-year-old Australian's comeback hit its stride over the last two weeks as she claimed the Nashville W15 and Lexington W50 titles back-to-back, the latter as a qualifier.

Giulia Safina Popa, +166 to No. 620: The 16-year-old Romanian compiled a 17-match winning streak over the past month, collecting three straight W15 titles in Campulung, Constanta and Varna before qualifying for the Burgas W50 last week. Popa, who qualified for her first WTA main draw as a 15-year-old last year in Iasi, is up to a new career high.

Ekaterina Dotsenko, +416 to No. 807: Dotsenko, the junior No. 21, has enjoyed an impressive start to her pro career. On her pro debut in July as a 14-year-old, she made a W15 final in Monastir; in her second and third events last month, she swept back-to-back W15 titles in the same venue, becoming the first 2011-born player to win a professional tournament. Dotsenko, who turned 15 years old last week, now becomes the first 2011-born player to reach the Top 1,000.

content.description: Zheng Qinwen made history as the first Chinese player to win the China Open, then celebrated her milestone win with some karaoke. Plus, Nikola Bartunkova had the breakthrough of her career. All that and more in the latest WTA week in review.

Zheng Qinwen makes history with China Open win in first title since 2024

content.body:
History was made in Beijing this past week, as Zheng Qinwen became the first Chinese player to win the China Open.

It was a dream tournament for Zheng, and a career highlight. But she wasn't the only player who shined in Beijing's second week. A 20-year-old cemented herself as one of the brightest rising stars on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz and two players qualified for the WTA Finals for the first time. Plus, we were treated to one of the most thrilling matches of the season.

Here's everything you need to know about what went down on tour last week, and the most important takeaways. 

Star of the Week

Zheng Qinwen

After some time away, Zheng Qinwen has officially returned to the upper tier of the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz.

Zheng won the biggest WTA title of her career, and her first since 2024, with an inspired performance in Beijing. And boy, did she earn it. In what has become a trend for the Olympic gold medalist, she won four consecutive three-setters to reach the quarterfinals, then upset sixth-seeded Elina Svitolina and 13th-seeded Elise Mertens to reach the final. She picked up another huge upset in the championship match, knocking off fourth-seeded Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 for her first WTA 1000 title.

Zheng, who got into the main draw as a wild card, is the lowest-ranked player ever to win the China Open, which dates back to 1994. (There was an eight-year hiatus between 1996 and 2004.) And she did it with an incredible display of power and controlled aggression. She had 243 winners in Beijing, the most of any player at any tournament since Aryna Sabalenka's 247 at the 2023 Australian Open. And her 51 aces trailed only Elena Rybakina's 54 at the US Open.

Speaking of the US Open, Zheng has now won 14 of her last 15 matches since the season's last major, where she reached the quarterfinals as a qualifier.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Breakthrough of the Week

Nikola Bartunkova

Coming into this tournament, 20-year-old Nikola Bartunkova had never been past the round of 16 at a WTA 1000 tournament. But the surging Czech star blew past that stage in Beijing, reaching the semifinals. She picked up the second and third Top 10 wins of her career along the way, upsetting Sabalenka in straight sets in the third round and then Karolina Muchova in the quarterfinals (more on that below).

After starting the season at No. 126 in the PIF WTA Rankings, she's now up to a career-high No. 29.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Best Match of the Week

Karolina Muchova d. Naomi Osaka, China Open round of 16

Muchova trailed by a break in both the first and third sets, but came back to outlast Naomi Osaka 7-5, 1-6, 7-6 (7) in a match that lasted 2 hours and 52 minutes. 

Muchova trailed 4-1 in the first set and 3-1 in the decider, and failed to convert triple match point at 5-4 in the third after five missed opportunities. She had three more match points in the tiebreaker, and finally clinched the match on her ninth match point with a backhand volley winner.

"I was shaking," a relieved Muchova said after the match.

Biggest Upset of the Week

Nikola Bartunkova d. Karolina Muchova, China Open quarterfinals

Jubilation was replaced with frustration in Muchova's next match, a dispiriting 6-3, 6-0 loss to Bartunkova in the quarterfinals.

As impressive as the win was for Bartunkova, what made it all the more surprising was the efficiency in which she delivered it. Bartunkova dropped just three games, including a second-set bagel, in just 67 minutes.

Within 20 minutes she was up 5-0 in the opener, and after Muchova fought back to make it interesting, Bartunkova won the final seven games to close out the dominant win.

Biggest Mover of the Week

Zheng Qinwen

Zheng rose 31 spots in the PIF WTA Rankings, to No. 23. Andreeva, 19, rose two spots to a career-high No. 3.

Social Moment of the Week

The karaoke queen

Biggest WTA title of her career? Check. History made on home soil? Check. Birthday week? Check. Return to the top 25? Check. Seems like as good a time as any to do some celebratory karaoke.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Tennis (@tennischannel)

And this wasn't the first time Zheng has shown off her karaoke skills. Cut to the United Cup two years ago.

Best Shot of the Week

Sara Bejlek's pass down the line

Sara Bejlek's speed and anticipation are her hallmarks, and they won her this point against Osaka.

Leading 4-3 in the first set, on Osaka's serve, Bejlek returned a combination of powerful backhands and forehands before winning the point with a remarkable pass down the line.

Must-Listen Podcast of the Week

Eala gets deep with Sharapova

Alexandra Eala was a guest on the "Pretty Tough with Maria Sharapova" podcast, and Eala discussed in great detail her relationship with perfection, navigating public opinion and managing pressure, and what makes her feel pretty and tough, among many other topics.

Check out their conversation below. 

Best Stat of the Week

15 hours

Zheng's four three-setters in seven matches, including four tiebreakers, kept her on court for 15 hours and 16 minutes. That's the most time spent on court by any player at any tournament this year, and the most since Opta began tracking total time spent on court in 2023. 

WTA Finals Update of the Week

Noskova, Andreeva punch their tickets

We have two more qualifiers! Andreeva and Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova have officially qualified for the WTA Finals at Indian Wells. 

They will both be making their WTA Finals singles debuts. (Andreeva qualified alongside Diana Shnaider in doubles last year.)

They join Sabalenka and Rybakina in the field, with four singles spots still up for grabs.

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

content.title: How humility and hard truths restored Zheng Qinwen’s fire in Beijing
content.description: For Zheng Qinwen, reclaiming her game required surviving a humbling six-month slump, swallowing pride in training and learning to balance hyper-aggressive tennis with composure under home-court pressure.

related.label: Zheng Qinwen's maturing perspective on success fuels energizing Beijing run
How one training block allowed Zheng to refind her game ahead of US Open
Zheng Qinwen makes history with China Open win in first title since 2024

content.body:
BEIJING -- During her China Open champion's press tour Sunday evening, Zheng Qinwen showed off an elegant, custom Nike dress designed dress in her favorite color, China red. 

In Chinese culture, red symbolizes prosperity, energy and celebration, fitting themes for Zheng’s historic victory in Beijing. She became the first home player to win the event and captured her first WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz 1000 title.

Sunday night’s championship was more than a milestone. It marked the high point of a humbling 2026 season for Zheng, whose resurgent form -- 13-1 in her past 14 tour-level matches -- has helped her put the past year in perspective.

"Finally after many losses, I find my fire again when I'm playing the [competitive matches]," Zheng said in press. "Like I always said, tennis is not just about hitting the balls, it's also about how much you want to win. I am just so grateful that I found the inside fire back. Right now, I'm trying to reach the best version of myself."

Before Zheng’s US Open quarterfinal run as a qualifier, the past year had been anything but prosperous, energetic or celebratory. She was still recovering from right elbow surgery in July 2025 and working to regain her form.

The injury and the results -- or lack thereof -- frustrated her. Zheng returned in Beijing last year but retired in the third round, having rushed back to the court before she was fully ready.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

It sidelined her until February in Doha, and she did not win three consecutive matches through Toronto, where she lost in the first round of qualifying. That low point helped Zheng develop a more mature perspective and accept the work required to rediscover her game: a rigorous training block, undertaken on the advice of coach Pere Riba.

"I thought the slump was one month, two months," Zheng said. "I did not expect it to be as long as six months. In the six months I was forced to learn a lot. Also I rediscovered myself. I knew that when I wasn't playing well, a lot of voices emerged. I learned to coexist with myself, to not be disrupted by those voices. All of those things make me stronger.

Zheng added that, in a letter to herself, she would stress the importance of staying humble in defeat and keeping her head up through a slump, with a reminder of all she had already achieved.

The US Open quarterfinal run and the China Open crown was the evidence of that turnaround, and her win in Beijing -- a tournament she dubs as the fifth Grand Slam -- brought her another prosperous, energetic and celebratory moment that she'd been looking for since her last title in 2024. 

After the final, wtatennis.com sat down with Zheng one-on-one. Here's more from the conversation:

After your success in 2024, you became a national icon for your country, and the win proved that even more. What's it like being so well-known in China?

Zheng: It's not easy to be a national icon. Since two, three years ago I felt high responsibility on my shoulder because I want to behave well in front of [my] people. I want those young kids when they look at me, I am a good inspiration for them. I want to be a good example for them because I know how much the example can make a huge impact for the kid.

I remember when I was a kid I used to watch Serena [Williams], this iconic player, how much impact they can [have on] me. I wish I could make always positive stuff with them.

In mid-June, you were ranked No. 160 and remarkably, you are now No. 23. How did the past few months rejuvenate your motivation?

Zheng: Since I come back from injury, I've always [been] really motivated, but in the beginning, sometimes at the important moment, I couldn't handle the pressure. [For a] long time, I wasn't handling pressure, and I'm wasn't used to it since I came back.

Finally, my ranking gets where I used to be. Still not there yet, but I'm on my way. I would just like to keep this hunger, stay humble and let's see what can come in the future because I feel like there's still so much more in me that I didn't put it out. I want to achieve my limits.

You accrued 243 winners this tournament, the most of any player at any tour-level event this season. As you showcased your best tennis all season, can you share how your aggressive style fueled your win?

Zheng: Oh, that’s interesting [smiling].

I always want to become an aggressive player, and the problem is sometimes when you are so aggressive, you make more unforced errors.  I learned that how to control my mistakes, and trying to find the right balance between making winners and controlling your unforced errors.

There's no place like home for Zheng Qinwen 🤩 #ChinaOpen https://t.co/7w8ZkSXBrh

— wta (@WTA) October 11, 2026

In this tournament, -- not only this one, but in the previous training before the tournament start -- I already started to make some game plan, trying to have a red spot in the training. Luckily I can show this in the match as well because sometimes you can play good in the practice match. Maybe you are not able to do that in a real match because all the pressure, all the emotion can affect how you impact the ball.

After facing so many losses, I finally felt that the pressure doesn't handle me anymore. I handle the pressure.

A huge figure in your journey has been your coach, Pere Riba. Could you expand more on his impact on you, particularly over the past few months where you reached one of your low points?

Zheng: It's true he made a huge change for me, and he saved me from the lowest moment when I lost that qualifying match in Toronto. Sometimes, it's really hard for his job as well, because if you want the player to perform as good, you need to be tough on court.

What’s happened in the past is maybe I was not humble enough to [hear] this hard [truths, this hard training, because I felt I'm already one of the best. I wanted to show that I know more than [him], and after many losses, I realized that's not the way.

If you want to win, you need to stay humble and listen to your coach, so I find in that moment I made a click and we've been working really well. He really did a lot of changes in my game -- also to my mental side -- because he's always the one who trusts me how much I can achieve. When I feel I'm at my limits, he's always there to push me more because he knows I have so much more in me that I can give on court.

There wasn’t an empty seat in the stadium tonight, a testament to your fandom. How did the atmosphere tonight compare to any other experience you’ve had on tour?

Zheng: China Open for me is like the fifth Grand Slam, and in this tournament, it's one of them I need to really give everything. I really appreciated today there is no empty seat, because I felt all the people that want to come to watch me play. I felt extra energy to fight there on court.

I always say that if I can reach [further rounds], people will know more about tennis. I know Chinese people, they like to see Chinese players compete because we have a big honor for our country, and I would really love more kids to know tennis, this sport. But no empty seats, that's quite amazing.

content.body:
Jessica Pegula may be getting a late start to her Asian swing, but the top-ranked American still has plenty to play for in the final weeks of the 2026 WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz season.

Sidelined since reaching the US Open semifinals after what she called a “long summer,” Pegula said she is healthy again and motivated to finish the year strong. She reached at least the semifinals in three of the four tournaments she played during the hard-court stretch following Wimbledon, ending with a loss to Aryna Sabalenka in New York.

Afterward, Pegula, 32, acknowledged the physical toll of her schedule and withdrew from Singapore and Beijing. She returns this week at the Dongfeng · Voyah Wuhan Open, where she is the defending finalist.

“Sometimes things can happen because of the accumulation of a lot of matches, playing a lot of tennis,” Pegula said ahead of the event.

View this post on Instagram

"When a big tournament finally ends, I think sometimes, for me at least, I start feeling a little bit run down. content.description: Zheng Qinwen became the first Chinese woman to win the China Open WTA 1000 title, defeating Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 for her first title at the level and sixth WTA Tour crown. The victory will lift Zheng back into the world's top 30, while Andreeva is projected to rise to No. 3 in the world

content.body:
Zheng Qinwen made history Sunday by becoming the first Chinese woman to win the China Open WTA 1000 title, defeating No. 4 seed Mirra Andreeva in straight sets.

Andreeva, who had lost the only previous meeting between the pair, broke early to take a 2-0 lead before Zheng fought back to level the set. Zheng then saved three set points in the 10th game of a closely contested set before winning the final 11 points in a row.

After the pair exchanged breaks early in the second set, Zheng earned a late break in the ninth game and held serve to complete the 7-5, 6-4 victory in 1 hour, 43 minutes.

"Honestly after winning this title, I felt like finally I achieve it, finally I once again become the one who is making new history," Zheng told the media. "I always wanted to kind of beat myself because everyone was asking me how great you achieve in 2024. I always say that the best is come in the future. 

The winning moment 🤩 History sealed with an ace from Zheng Qinwen! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/U9tSRpv7KN

— wta (@WTA) October 11, 2026
Impressive stats behind Zheng's historic run

It was Zheng's first WTA 1000 title and her sixth overall on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz. It was also her first title since winning in Tokyo in late 2024. The victory will see her return to the top 30 in the world rankings next week, having fallen to No. 160 midway through the season.

"When I was at the lowest moment, everyone was saying I couldn't come back," Zheng said. "Everyone had doubts about me. Finally after many losses, I was able to find my fire again when I'm playing matches. Like I always said, tennis is not just about hitting the balls, it's also about how much you want to win. I am just so grateful that I found the inside fire back. Right now I'm trying to reach the best version of myself."

The 24-year-old, currently ranked No. 54 in the world, became the first wildcard to win the event since the tournament's reinauguration in 2004. She also became the lowest-ranked player to win the title during that span.

After winning her first four matches at the tournament in three sets, Zheng won her final three matches in straight sets. The 78 games she dropped en route to the title were the most by a player winning a Tier I or WTA 1000 event since the format was introduced in 1990, surpassing the 66 dropped by Belinda Bencic in Toronto in 2015. Only Madison Keys, who dropped 87 games at the Australian Open in 2025, has dropped more games en route to winning a WTA-level title in the Open Era.

"Every match had different difficult points," Zheng said looking back at her matches in Beijing. "It is difficult to pinpoint which moment was the most difficult. The final tonight was also difficult. Also the previous six matches were tough. There were different moments of toughness. When I was battling my opponents, I was also battling myself.

"The desire of winning internally, I was battling the internal weaknesses of myself. I need to be aggressive, but also need to control my errors. At critical moments, I cannot be soft. This is something I really need to find solution for for a long time. I'm really happy I did that."

The victory over Andreeva, who is projected to rise to No. 3 in the rankings Monday, was also Zheng's 14th career win over a top-10 opponent and her third this season.

Andreeva  third-youngest this century to reach the top 3

Andreeva credited Zheng for delivering a strong performance in the final and expects more success for the former world No. 4 in the coming months.

"I just think, of course, she's a great server. I also think today I missed a lot of returns trying to go for it, trying to be more aggressive. Sometimes it worked, but most of the time I just felt like, I wanted to go for it but couldn't really find I guess the margin, couldn't really find the rhythm, as well.

"I will probably need to look at this match and just see why, try to improve and learn from that. For sure today she played great. She also mentioned, of course we all know, that she's had a tough year. It's also very nice to see her playing better and coming back. I think that she's going to be raising her level even more soon."

Zheng herself believes there is more to come from her.

"I can't give exactly number how close I am to the best version of myself," she added. "But it is true, I achieved something that I never achieved before when I was at my 21 years old. I know everyone is saying, I never had a 1000 event title. I was Olympic gold medalist, that's amazing, but still there's lot of things I have never achieved yet.

"I want to achieve all of them, like these people cannot say anything to me after that. I'm really happy I made the first steps. For me there's still more to come. I'm so hungry honestly for what's going to come in the next of my career because I know my potential, and I don't want to have a regret the day that I retire from tennis. I just want to give everything that I have in the tennis career."

Despite the loss, Andreeva will become the third-youngest player this century to reach the top three of the WTA rankings for the first time, behind only Maria Sharapova and Kim Clijsters.

"I think overall of course it was a good tournament," Andreeva said. "I mean, a lot of positives to take from these two weeks. Of course, I felt like today just wasn't meant to be. I think after also talking with Conchita, I will be able to look onto this match maybe from a different perspective and see maybe some good things."

content.body:
No. 2 seeds Gabriela Dabrowski and Luisa Stefani won the China Open in Beijing on Sunday, defeating top seeds Katerina Siniakova and Zhang Shuai in straight sets.

Dabrowski and Stefani needed just 59 minutes to beat Siniakova and Zhang 6-1, 6-2 and claim their seventh overall title as a team. It was their fifth title of the season, following victories in Dubai, Strasbourg, Eastbourne and São Paulo. 

"Proud of a lot really," Dabrowski said to press. "Obviously today's performance was a really great culmination of the entire week, which was awesome for us. We brought a really high level. Our opponents forced us to do that with their reputation, the number of times we've played them."

The winning moment 🤩 Gabriela Dabrowski & Luisa Stefani are your champions in Beijing! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/CfGwE5ee7x

— wta (@WTA) October 11, 2026
"Job not finished" says Stefani as the season heads to its final month

For Dabrowski, the victory marked her 25th career tour-level doubles title and seventh at a WTA 1000 event. Stefani claimed her 18th career doubles title and fifth at the WTA 1000 level. The pair improved their tour-level record as a team to 75-19.

"I think for me it's still kind of in the middle of it. It kind of feels like job's not finished in terms of the season still going," Stefani said reflecting on their season. "I have a lot of pride. I'm very grateful for everything that we've been accomplishing and how well we've been playing, how we've improved together since the beginning of the year.

"What the process has been like, too, in terms of our team effort, and not just Gabby and I, but our team as well who are guiding us and helping us be better as a team. I think it's really cool to see that come to light in how we execute and how we perform. Then we get results from it. We're almost in November. To be healthy and playing well, winning a title here, also means a lot. Like I said, there's still a little bit more to go. I'm trying to focus on what we're doing and still enjoying staying present and staying in the moment."

Gaby & Luisa rising to the challenge 👏 #ChinaOpen https://t.co/2I3ZfkTfqH

— wta (@WTA) October 11, 2026
"I don't feel a bit that I want to leave this community" - 37-year-old Zhang

For Siniakova and Zhang, this was their sixth tour-level event as a team. They first partnered at the 2024 Guangzhou Open, winning the title, and have since claimed two more championships together, at Adelaide and Toronto, both this year.

Their defeat in Beijing was their first loss as a team this year, ending a 13-match winning streak. They now have a 19-3 record as a pair.

"I think they were serving well," Siniakova said. "When you're serving 180 [KM/H], 160 second serve, it's tough to do something, especially when they are both really good at the net. I think we tried everything, but we were just missing by a bit. Of course, to compare it against them when they were really on fire and everything kind of were going their ways, it was very tough to find some space to do anything or to change anything."

At 37, Zhang is enjoying one of her most successful seasons on tour and spoke about why she remains committed to competing on the tour.

"This year I have been healthy: healthy body, healthy mindset," she said. "I keep fighting till now. I can be with my good friends to be in the doubles in different events. Deep runs in those events. I feel that on the WTA Tour, this community is like a family for me.

"These players, the staff members, people working here, it makes me happy. I don't feel a bit that I want to leave this community. I really treasure the time here, every tournament, every event. We see those people, local people, trying their best to try to support these events. That makes me want to stay in the sport. I have the motivation to continue to stay on the tour, to continue to try my best in this sport. I feel the urge and passion for it."

content.title: Zheng becomes first Chinese finalist in Beijing with straight-sets win over Mertens
content.description: Zheng Qinwen became the first ever Chinese finalist in Beijing on Saturday, defeating No. 13 seed Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2. The Olympic gold medalist won eight of the final 10 games to book a spot in the title match against Mirra Andreeva.
content.body:
Zheng Qinwen made history Saturday night in Beijing, defeating No. 13 seed Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2 in 1 hour, 32 minutes to become the first Chinese player to reach the China Open final.

Beijing: Scores | Order of play | Draws

Chinese players had previously gone 0-7 in semifinals at the event, but Zheng ended that drought with a commanding performance. The Olympic gold medalist started fast and withstood a late surge from Mertens in the opening set before winning eight of the final 10 games to close out the match.

The victory sends Zheng to the 11th WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz final of her career and her second at the WTA 1000 level.

"The China Open treats me really well," Zheng said in her post-match interview. "I always want to give my best here. It's like the fifth Grand Slam for me. I just really want to give everything I have for this stadium."

Final bound ⭐️ Zheng Qinwen makes history defeating Mertens 7-5, 6-2 and advancing to the Beijing final! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/KQmilZAmkw

— wta (@WTA) October 10, 2026

Zheng will have one more opportunity to play in front of the home crowd when she faces No. 4 seed Mirra Andreeva in the final. The 19-year-old advanced earlier Saturday with a 6-2, 6-2 victory over Nikola Bartunkova in a matchup of young stars.

Zheng won her only previous meeting with Andreeva, rallying from a set down in the 2024 China Open quarterfinals.

"I think for sure in these [last] two years, both of us, we became more mature," Zheng said in her post-match press conference. "She just won Roland Garros this year. It was a really great achievement for her.

"She's always a tough opponent because she's always there fighting. A very consistent player. I would say it is not an easy match, but I'm also a tough player. Tomorrow is going to be a hard battle."

Drawn-out charge to the final

Entering as a wild card, Zheng's path to the final was anything but easy. Each of her first four matches went to a third set, including victories over No. 15 seed Anna Kalinskaya, No. 18 seed Marie Bouzkova and Alina Charaeva, who stunned Elena Rybakina earlier in the tournament.

She then defeated No. 6 seed Elina Svitolina in straight sets to reach the semifinals, where she dispatched Mertens to set up a showdown with Andreeva.

"I would say the more matches I play, the more free, better tennis I achieve because I'm that kind of player," Zheng said. "My limits are really high, so I need to find out my rhythm from the beginning of the tournament. Luckily, I've been playing some really aggressive tennis because that's the goal I had for myself."

Along the way, Zheng continued to unleash winners from all corners of the court. She struck 32 against Mertens while committing just 16 unforced errors, good for a 2-to-1 ratio. Her 219 winners thus far in Beijing are the most by any player at a single WTA event this season, surpassing Karolina Muchova's 210 at Wimbledon.

Since Opta began tracking the statistic in 2021, Zheng is just the third player to hit 200 or more winners at a WTA 1000 event, joining Aryna Sabalenka (231 in Madrid in 2024) and Elena Rybakina (204 in Miami in 2024).

Zheng also surpassed Muchova for the most time spent on court at a single WTA event this year, logging 13 hours, 33 minutes through six matches.

And for good measure: At No. 54 in the PIF WTA Rankings, Zheng is the lowest-ranked player to reach the China Open final since 2004, surpassing No. 49 Muchova, who reached the championship match in 2024. She is also the first wild card to reach the final since 2004.

content.title: Andreeva or Zheng? Making the case for the China Open finalists
content.description: Zheng Qinwen, the first Chinese finalist in Beijing, will play Mirra Andreeva for the China Open title. We make the case for both players.

related.label: Andreeva advances to fifth final of 2026 in Beijing, set to become World No. 3
Zheng Qinwen's maturing perspective on success fuels energizing Beijing run
Andreeva vs. Zheng: Everything to know about the Beijing final

content.body:
History was made in Beijing on Saturday when Zheng Qinwen defeated Elise Mertens to become the first Chinese finalist in the history of the China Open, which dates back to 2004.

Zheng won eight of the final 10 games against Mertens to reach her second career WTA 1000 final, building on a resurgent two months that could propel her back into the Top 30 of the PIF WTA Rankings.

She'll play Mirra Andreeva in the final on Sunday. Andreeva breezed past rising star Nikola Bartunkova 6-2, 6-2, and she'll be playing for her third WTA 1000 title.

Ahead of the championship match in Beijing, we make the case for both players.

The Case for Mirra Andreeva

It's all coming up roses for Andreeva, who will be the clear favorite in this final. The fourth seed has now won 10 consecutive sets in Beijing, and she was clinical in her semifinal win over Bartunkova, dropping just four games against a player having the tournament of her career. Andreeva was steady and efficient, with 16 winners and 10 unforced errors, and continued her excellence on return, a point of emphasis for Andreeva and her team of late.

The World No. 5, who qualified for the WTA Finals on Friday and is set to rise to a career-high No. 3 in the PIF WTA Rankings next week, converted five of her 10 break-point opportunities. That brings her total to 301 on the season, which leads the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz.

Despite being just 19, Andreeva also comes into this match with the edge in experience on the biggest stages. This will be her fifth title match of the season, and she's already won three of them, including her first major title at Roland Garros. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Andreeva also figures to be the fresher and more well-rested player, coming off a brisk 1 hour and 14 minute semifinal and four consecutive straight-set matches. She's played five fewer sets than Zheng, whose 13 hours and 33 minutes on court are the most of any player at any event this season.

On Sunday, the crowd will surely be behind Zheng when they step onto Diamond Court. Andreeva understands that, and will be ready for it. It won't be the first time she's had to manage that kind of environment.

"I have some experience playing against local players," Andreeva told reporters. "I think that's going to be fine. Of course, we all know that she's playing at home. That's OK."

The Case for Zheng Qinwen

Even if Andreeva is unfazed by playing Zheng on her home soil, it will surely give the World No. 54 a tremendous boost in the title match, as it has all tournament.

Zheng, who got into the draw as a wild card, fought her way through four consecutive three-set matches to start the tournament, two of which were upsets of Anna Kalinskaya and Marie Bouzkova. And despite the toll that those marathons surely took on her, they appear to have only made her stronger and more confident. Zheng's wins over Elina Svitolina and Mertens were in straights, and in the latter match Zheng looked the part of a former Top 5 player. She was aggressive but controlled, with 32 winners to 16 unforced errors, and her serve was a weapon, winning 73 percent of her service points (including 88 percent of first-serve points) and hitting eight aces.

On her return, she only faced two break points.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Zheng's service games will put Andreeva's defense to the test. She's hit 219 winners in her six matches, the highest amount of any player at any tournament this season. And her 47 aces in Beijing are third, behind just Elena Rybakina's 54 at the US Open and 49 in Toronto.

Dating back to the start of the US Open, following the training block in Florida that completely transformed her season, Zheng has won 13 of her last 14 matches.

Zheng will also have the confidence of a previous win against Andreeva, at this very tournament. In 2024, in their lone meeting on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, she beat Andreeva 5-7, 6-0, 6-4 in the China Open quarterfinals.

content.body:
BEIJING -- A new China Open champion is set to be crowned.

No. 4 seed Mirra Andreeva is in search of her fourth title of 2026, and will be put to the test against home favorite and wild card Zheng Qinwen, who is seeking her first title on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz since Tokyo in 2024. 

Their lone previous meeting came in Beijing two years ago, a Zheng 5-7, 6-0, 6-4 comeback win in the quarterfinals.

From the order of play and head-to-head history to prize money and more, here's everything you need to know about Sunday's China Open final.

When is the Beijing singles final?

The singles final concludes play on Capital Group Diamond Court Sunday evening and will begin, not before 7:30 p.m., following the doubles final.

The doubles final will begin at 4:30 p.m. local, and features the duo of Katerina Siniakova and Zhang Shuai, who await either Gabriel Dabrowski and Luisa Stefani or Elise Mertens and Diana Shnaider.

Time conversions for singles final: NB 7:30 a.m. EST , 12:30 p.m. CEST 

How did each singles player reach the championship?

Andreeva
First round: Bye
Second round: def. Yuan Yue 3-6, 6-0, 6-0
Third round: def. Polina Kudermetova 6-4, 6-1
Fourth round: def. Daria Snigur 6-2, 6-2
Quarterfinal: def. [19] Ekaterina Alexandrova 7-6(4), 7-6(3)
Semifinal: def. [26] Nikola Bartunkova 6-2, 6-2

Andreeva is into her fifth final of 2026, with titles at Roland Garros, Adelaide and Linz and a runner-up finish in Madrid. Her five final appearances is tied with Elena Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka and Jessica Pegula.

Zheng
First round: def. Shi Han 7-6(6), 4-6, 6-2
Second round: def. [15] Anna Kalinskaya 6-7(4), 6-0, 3-0 ret.
Third round: def. [18] Marie Bouzkova 7-6(3), 4-6, 7-5
Fourth round: def. Alina Charaeva 6-2, 2-6, 6-4
Quarterfinal: def. [6] Elina Svitolina 6-3, 7-6(6)
Semifinal: def. [13] Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2

Since the China Open's beginning in 2004 on the WTA Tour, no Chinese player has won the title. Zheng is also the first player from China to reach the final, after Chinese players were 0-7 in semifinals prior. 

What are the ranking points and prize money at stake?

In Beijing, a total of USD $9,415,725 was available in prize money, and the singles champion will receive $1,151,380. The finalist will take home $612,340. In doubles, the winning duo splits $468,200 and runners-up earn $247,870.

As with all WTA 1000 events, 1000 ranking points are on the table in both the PIF WTA Rankings and the Race to the WTA Finals at Indian Wells, while the runner-up earns 650 points. Any change in rank is based on how the player performs in the tournament compared to the points earned in the same week last year. 

Regardless of the result, Andreeva is projected to be the new World No. 3 in the PIF WTA Rankings on Monday, and she has already qualified for the WTA Finals at Indian Wells. 

As for Zheng, she was ranked No. 160 in mid-June, but after a tremendous summer and early fall, she's projected to be back into the top 30.

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

By the numbers

Andreeva

10: After dropping her opening set of the tournament, Andreeva has won the next 10. 

50: With her semifinal win, Andreeva has won 50 matches this season. Andreeva, 19, is the youngest player to reach that mark since Caroline Wozniacki in 2009. She's tied with Pegula for most wins this season.

301: Andreeva has converted 25 break point opportunities in Beijing, adding to her cumulative total of 301 on the season. She's the first player in 2026 to eclipse the 300 mark. 

Watch the Match Highlights from Qinwen Zheng vs. Elise Mertens from the Semifinal in Beijing. #WTA #tennis #ChinaOpen #Beijing https://t.co/oVR5s4LlgY

— wta (@WTA) October 10, 2026

Zheng

2: Since 1990, Zheng, Wuhan 2024 and Beijing 2026, is just the second to reach her first two career Tier I/WTA 1000 finals in her home country -- Serena Williams, Indian Wells and Miami 1999.

13: Zheng has spent 13 hours and 33 minutes on court, the most of any player at a single tour-level event this season. The next most is Karolina Muchova with 13 hours and 3 minutes at Wimbledon.

219: Zheng has already amassed 219 winners this tournament, the most of any player at a single tour-level event this season. She passed Muchova's 210 at Wimbledon.

What they had to say?

Andreeva

1. "I pretty much have some experience of playing against local players. I think that's going to be fine. Of course, we all know that she's playing at home. Also she's been coming back, she's been playing better, she's been beating a lot of great players.

"I feel like Qinwen -- obviously she's more aggressive, she likes to hit a lot of balls, she tries to play fast. We will prepare our best with Conchita no matter who will win and I will try to play my best in the final."

2. "I think especially here this tournament -- also we take my first match where it was kind of up and down a lot, felt like I didn't play my best --I  just felt with every match that I've been playing, I was feeling better and better physically and mentally [with] the way I was playing on court."

Zheng

1. "I'm always proud to play in front of my home crowd. I always wants to show my best level in front of them because I know how much they support me. So I felt like I don't want to let them down. Also I don't want to let myself down.

"In a way it's a pressure, but in the same time it gives me motivation. I just need to use them in the right way."

2. "For sure in these two years both of us, we [have] become more mature. She just won Roland Garros this year, a really great achievement for her. I think she's always tough opponent because she's always there fighting, very consistent player. It is not easy match, but also I'm a tough player. Tomorrow is going to be a hard battle."

content.body:
A day after securing her berth in the season-ending WTA Finals, No. 4 seed Mirra Andreeva advanced to the China Open final in Beijing for the first time with a straight-sets victory over No. 26 seed Nikola Bartunkova.

Andreeva needed 1 hour, 14 minutes to secure the 6-2, 6-2 victory, hitting 16 winners and committing just 10 unforced errors in the semifinal.

"I'm very happy and excited to be in the finals," Andreeva told the media after the win. "I think I played very good today. I'm super happy with the way I was playing. Of course, Nikola is a very tricky opponent. We had a tough match at the US Open. But I'm super happy I won today."

Storming into the final ⚡️ Mirra Andreeva closes out an incredible performance defeating Bartunkova 6-2, 6-2 and reaches the final in Beijing! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/NhvaPVNUc9

— wta (@WTA) October 10, 2026

Andreeva revealed that she has been working with her team on several aspects of her game, particularly her return. The work is paying off. She leads the WTA Tour in break points converted in 2026, having converted 301 in main-draw matches at tour level this season. She converted five in Saturday's semifinal from 10 break-point opportunities.

"We've been working on returning a lot," she added. "Every practice that I have we're trying to improve everything, but also to work on return because I feel like even if the opponent serves well, you still have to try and put some pressure on the server. I feel like the work is paying off little by little. So super happy with those numbers. Conchita will be even more happy because it was her initiative. We'll just continue improving (smiling)."

Sunday's final will be Andreeva's fifth of the season, tying her with Elena Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka and Jessica Pegula for the most finals appearances this year on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz.

The victory was Andreeva's 50th of the season, tying her with Pegula for the most match wins on the tour in 2026. The result will also lift her to a career-high World No. 3 in the rankings next week.

Andreeva will face No. 13 seed Elise Mertens or former World No. 4 Zheng Qinwen in Sunday's final. She has lost her only previous match against Zheng and holds a 1-0 record against Mertens.

"I think if Qinwen wins, I pretty much have some experience of playing against local players," Andreeva said looking ahead to Sunday. "I think that's going to be fine. We all know that she's playing at home. Also she's been coming back, she's been playing better, she's been beating a lot of great players. I think no matter who's going to win, it's going to be tough. I think Elise, she beat two top-10 players in a row. She's also on a great winning streak. She's been playing great, as well."

Despite their different playing styles, Andreeva said she and her team will be prepared for the final. "Elise has a different game style," she added. "I feel like Qinwen, obviously she's more aggressive, she likes to hit a lot of balls, she tries to play fast, whereas I think Elise kind of likes to play, build the point, kind of be smart, what to do. Different types of opponents. We will prepare our best with Conchita no matter who will win and I will try to play my best in the final."

We've reached the business end of the China Open, the second-to-last WTA 1000 tournament of the season.

The 96-player singles draw is down to the final four, with WTA Finals qualifier Mirra Andreeva taking on rising star Nikola Bartunkova for a spot in the championship match. In the second semifinal on Saturday, home favorite Zheng Qinwen will play Elise Mertens.

We've rounded up our favorites from Week 2, including highlights from Sun Xinran, Jelena Ostapenko and Sara Bejlek. Check them out below, and make sure to vote for your WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz shot of the week at the bottom.

Sun Xinran's running forehand pass

Sun caught the attention of many fans this week, both for her two impressive wins in her WTA debut and sparkling shots like this one. 

Serving to take a 3-2 lead against Coco Gauff, Sun returned a booming crosscourt backhand from Gauff, then sprinted to the service line and hit a running forehand pass.

Gauff won the match 7-5, 6-1.

Jelena Ostapenko's pickup volley off her shoelaces

Serving at 2-4, 15-all in the decisive third set against Mertens, Ostapenko dictated the point from the net, forcing Mertens to defend from behind the baseline. Mertens stayed in the point with some stellar returns, but Ostapenko won it with a pickup volley off her shoelaces.

Mertens ended up playing better down the stretch, pulling out the 6-2, 3-6, 6-3 win.

Marie Bouzkova's counter drop shot on the run

Marie Bouzkova showed off her incredible court coverage and variety in this point against Zheng, finishing it off with a sweet counter drop shot.

Zheng outlasted Bouzkova 7-6 (3), 4-6, 7-5.

Kamilla Rakhimova's full-stretch backhand winner

Iva Jovic gave Kamilla Rakhimova all she could handle in this point, both with punishing blows and awkward spins. But Rakhimova won the battle of angles with a full-stretch backhand winner into the open court. 

Jovic won the match 6-1, 7-5.

Sara Bejlek's pass down the line

Bejlek's speed and anticipation are her hallmarks, and they won her this point against Naomi Osaka.

Leading 4-3 in the first set, on Osaka's serve, Bejlek returned a combination of powerful backhands and forehands before winning the point with a remarkable pass down the line.

content.title: Mertens beats Swiatek in Beijing for third straight win over a Grand Slam champion
content.description: Elise Mertens has now defeated three straight Grand Slam champions at the China Open, and her win over Iga Swiatek also secured WTA Finals berths for Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova.

related.label: Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova secure qualification for WTA Finals Indian Wells
Zheng’s late-season surge continues with win over Svitolina to reach Beijing semis

content.body:
Elise Mertens continued her impressive run of form Friday night in Beijing, upsetting No. 8 seed Iga Swiatek 7-6 (0), 6-3 in 1 hour and 50 minutes to reach the China Open semifinals for the first time.

Beijing: Scores | Order of play | Draws

The victory was Mertens' first over Swiatek in three WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz meetings and sent the Belgian into her first WTA 1000 singles semifinal since 2021 and third overall. Her path has been anything but easy, as she has defeated three consecutive Grand Slam champions: Jelena Ostapenko, Coco Gauff and now Swiatek.

ANOTHER BIG WIN IN BEIJING!🤩 @elise_mertens defeats Swiatek in straight sets! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/iypSchMkip

— wta (@WTA) October 9, 2026

Mertens has now defeated three Grand Slam champions at a single WTA event for the first time in her career. The only previous tournament in which she beat multiple Major champions came during her title run in Doha in 2019, when she defeated Angelique Kerber in the semifinals and Simona Halep in the final.

"Sometimes you just grow into a tournament," Mertens told reporters. "My second round, [Katie Volynets] already played a match and she kind of knew the circumstances. [It was] my first match, and you have to feel the ball a little bit. Then yeah, Ostapenko, she can play some good tennis, too. No easy rounds."

With victories over Gauff and Swiatek, Mertens also became the first player to defeat multiple former China Open champions at a single edition of the tournament since Aryna Sabalenka in 2018.

Swiatek's loss also clinched WTA Finals Indian Wells berths for Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova. Both players, fresh off maiden Grand Slam titles at Roland Garros and Wimbledon, respectively, will make their singles debuts at the year-end championships.

Heading to the WTA Finals Indian Wells 👏 Mirra Andreeva has confirmed her place on #TheUltimateStage! Get your tickets to see Mirra take to the court 👉 https://t.co/XSKV4xqvlZ #WTAFinals https://t.co/dKBi7WxyA2

— wta (@WTA) October 9, 2026

Qualification CONFIRMED 👊 Linda Noskova will take to #TheUltimateStage! Grab your tickets to WTA Finals Indian Wells: https://t.co/6YTn8O1CTv #WTAFinals https://t.co/NK6BGrPNBl

— wta (@WTA) October 9, 2026
Mertens near-perfect in victory

Despite the storylines surrounding the match, Mertens was the star of the day with a near-flawless performance against Swiatek.

The numbers tell the story: Mertens won 87% of her first-serve points (33 of 38), hit 24 winners against just 11 unforced errors and did not face a break point. For reference, Mertens is just the second player not to face a single break point against Swiatek in a WTA Tour main-draw match -- excluding Grand Slams, team events and the Olympics -- after Coco Gauff in Madrid in 2025.

But that's not all. After trading holds throughout the opening set, in which Mertens held two break points but was unable to convert, the set was decided by a tiebreak. And while Swiatek is more often the one handing out bagels, it was Mertens who dominated the tiebreak, winning it 7-0 for a mini-bagel.

Just an edge above 🔥 @elise_mertens takes the lead against Swiatek 7-6(0) after a tight opening set! #ChinaOpen https://t.co/497UboBBhU

— wta (@WTA) October 9, 2026

Mertens is the first player to claim a tiebreak to love against Swiatek at the WTA level.

The match continued in Mertens' favor in the second set. She finally converted a break point to take a 3-1 lead before consolidating with a love hold for 4-1. Swiatek had one last opportunity to strike back after taking a 0-30 lead in the final game, but Mertens won four consecutive points to close out the victory.

What's next

The win leaves Mertens with a tough assignment in the semifinals, where she'll face local star Zheng Qinwen after the former Olympic gold medalist defeated No. 6 seed Elina Svitolina 6-3, 7-6 (8) earlier Friday.

The two have met once before, a three-set encounter in Charleston last season won by Zheng.

"She's an incredible player. She's been a Top 10 player," Mertens said. "Of course, [she was] unlucky with the injury, but her level is there. It's going to be a great match. She has a home advantage, but still I'm enjoying my time here in Beijing. I'm still in singles and doubles. I'm going to give 100% again."

Should Mertens prevail in the rematch, she would advance to her first WTA 1000 singles final. Since the format's introduction in 2009, Mertens could become the second-oldest player to reach a maiden WTA 1000 final, younger only than Flavia Pennetta at Indian Wells in 2014.

Mertens and partner Diana Shnaider are also through to the doubles semifinals. They are scheduled to face No. 2 seeds Gabriela Dabrowski and Luisa Stefani following Mertens' singles semifinal on Saturday.

content.body:
China’s Zheng Qinwen advanced to the semifinals of the China Open WTA 1000 in Beijing with a 6-3, 7-6 (8-6) upset victory over No. 6 seed Elina Svitolina.

In her first tournament since reaching the US Open quarterfinals as a qualifier, Zheng continued her strong late-season run, winning 12 of her last 13 matches on tour.

Zheng opened the match with a break of serve to take a 2-0 lead and broke twice more to claim the first set 6-3. The second set was much closer, with neither player dropping serve, forcing a tiebreak. Zheng converted her second match point to complete the victory in 1 hour, 47 minutes.

"It was a really great win for me," Zheng told the media after the match. "I think she also play her best tennis. I'm just happy to have lot of winners during the match, and at the end, be brave in important moment. I finish with really good winners."

Eight of Zheng's 12 recent victories have come in three sets. She credited the hard work during a training block she put in before the US Open for her recent success.

"What I did in that training block is still unforgettable," she said. "I've been facing a lot of tough physical conditions. Not only the weather, the training, but mentally. I needed that training block. I need to accept when the coach, they are hard to me on court. I remember Pere, he say to me,

"Right now you are just 140 in the ranking. So now you need to listen to me more on court because you are not the top 10 you were. I was really angry inside. But I have to calm down and say yes, that's the reality. Seems like the effort pays off. Honestly, I didn't expect that, all this coming, because I'm just really focused on the present."

The victory took Zheng to her fourth career WTA 1000 semifinal and her third on Chinese soil, following appearances in Beijing and Wuhan in 2024. The former world No. 4 is projected to return to the top 40 in the WTA PIF Rankings after falling to No. 160 in June.

Zheng has become the third wild-card entry to reach the semifinals, following Shuai Peng in 2006 and Qiang Wang in 2018. She is also the third Chinese player to reach the tournament's semifinals more than once, after Li Na and Peng.

Zheng will face the winner of the quarterfinal between No. 8 seed Swiatek and No. 13 seed Elise Mertens. The 24-year-old won her only previous meeting with Mertens and holds a 2-7 record against Swiatek.

"I think those important two matches I beat [Swiatek] is because I was more consistent" Zheng said. "I remember those matches when I lost against her, it's because she's more consistent than me. We were really close. We face each other lot of times. Doesn't matter who I face. I'm sure if they arrive to semifinal, they will show up with their best tennis. I'm just going to stay there and play my tennis and let's see what's going to happen."

content.title: Zheng Qinwen's maturing perspective on success fuels energizing Beijing run
content.description: Zheng Qinwen's latest run in Beijing is more than just the result. Returning to the site of a 2025 low point, she reflected on how subsequent lows reshaped her mindset and taught her to find value ahead of the final stretch of the 2026 season.
content.body:
BEIJING -- Zheng Qinwen used to think winning was like "water."

Every single match, she had to win because earlier in her career, winning was viewed as essential and a necessity to sustain life on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz. Winning was seen as the norm, and that made it difficult navigating low points at times. 

Now, particularly over the past few months, that viewpoint has changed. A day after she celebrated her 24th birthday, Zheng spoke on her maturing mindset as she enters her second career China Open semifinal following her win over Elina Svitolina in Friday's quarterfinal.

"I'm more grateful for every win because I understand how much effort I have made behind every win," Zheng said. "I've learned to enjoy the wins and the effort on court."

Of course, winning is important for rankings, prize money and capturing titles, but Zheng isn't riding or dying on it. Rather, she's come to appreciate the work behind the scenes and that low points in her career are not a negative thing, a lesson that she learned over the past few months. 

"My biggest takeaway is that lows are not necessarily bad," Zheng said. "Being positive every day is really difficult. When I am low, I have the energy to make a breakthrough. I saw the shortcomings in myself. I saw the weaknesses of my personality. The lows actually helped me improve.

"When you are in the lows, you should face the challenge. That's what helps you reflect and grow because you'll always make it back from the lows."

The China Open is particularly personal to Zheng, not just because she's performing in front of her home crowd, but rather it was the location of one of her lows last season. 

In Beijing in 2025, she retired from her third-round match with a right-elbow injury that had kept her out since Wimbledon because of the surgery. After that retirement, she didn't play again until Doha in February.

Eventually, because she wasn't playing at her highest level and getting results, the former World No. 4's ranking slipped to as low as No. 160 and she became reliant on wild cards for direct entry.

Then came Toronto, where a qualifying loss sparked the turning point of her season arguably when Zheng was at her lowest. At the push of her team, Zheng underwent an intense training block in Florida to rediscover her game and skipped Cincinnati. Since, she's posted her two best results all season with quarterfinals at the US Open and is now into the final four in Beijing. 

Simply, Zheng just needed to accept to herself that winning wasn't essential at that point in her time, and it's paid off. Zheng is 12-1 in main-draw matches since Toronto, including the three US Open qualifiers.

"What I did in that training block is still unforgettable," Zheng said. "I couldn't play those tournaments. I [had] to accept [that] I needed this training block. I need to accept when the coach, they are hard to me on court.

"I remember [my coach] Pere [Riba], he said to me: 'Right now you are just 140 in the ranking. You used to be 65 before. You need to listen to me more on court because you are not the top 10 you [once were].' I was really angry inside. But I have to calm down and say yes, that's the reality. Seems like the effort [has paid off]."

" When you are in the lows, you should face the challenge. That's what helps you reflect and grow because you'll always make it back from the lows. "
Zheng Qinwen during her post-quarterfinal press conference in Beijing

At the time, Zheng didn't expect that the results would come this quickly, admitting she was "too low" to look at the future. 

Experiencing low points is a part of every tennis player's career, and Zheng is no different. However, with her recovery and journey back onto the WTA Tour taking longer than expected, it made her appreciate the larger picture.

"Going through this journey, there have been many chapters. I could write many chapters," Zheng said. "You see the lows in the recent period, but in my junior years, there were many highs and lows. It's been like this all the way through.

"I didn't expect that the lows this time continued that long. That is why I treasure the opportunities now."
